title: National Tire Dealers & Retreaders Association v. Brinegar (1974)
shortTitle: National Tire Dealers & Retreaders Association v. Brinegar (1974)
summary: A tire-labeling rule lacked an adequate explanation of practicability and safety benefits, except where Congress itself required permanent labels.

sections.Parties: The National Tire Dealers and Retreaders Association challenged the Secretary of Transportation’s requirements for permanently molding information into retreaded passenger tires.
sections.Material Facts: Standard No. 117 required permanent sidewall information including size, pressure, load, ply characteristics, and tire construction. The association accepted the value of point-of-sale information but opposed permanently molding all those facts into used casings. Existing markings often disappeared during buffing, and frequently changing plates in hot molds created cost and safety problems. Industry comments predicted that using only suitably marked casings would sharply reduce available inventory and that relabeling could increase costs substantially. The agency asserted that existing labeling techniques and sorting could solve the problems without supporting those assertions adequately in the record.
sections.Procedural History: The association petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review of the promulgated standard. The court considered the administrative record, the agency’s explanation, and its denial of reconsideration. It set aside the discretionary permanent-labeling requirements while retaining requirements expressly commanded by Congress.
sections.Issue: Did the record establish that the discretionary permanent-labeling requirements were practicable and sufficiently connected to motor-vehicle safety, as the Safety Act required?
sections.Holding: The court vacated the portions concerning permanent labels for tire size, maximum inflation pressure, ply rating, tubeless or tube-type status, and bias-belted or radial construction. Requirements for actual number of plies and maximum permissible load remained because the statute commanded them. The court also observed that the agency lacked power to omit Congress’s required disclosure of ply material.
sections.Reasoning: The relevant comparison was permanent labeling versus an affixed label, rather than information versus no information. Permanent information might assist later purchasers or matching replacement tires, but the agency supplied little support about the frequency or practical importance of those situations. Meanwhile, the comments raised serious practicability objections that a bare assertion of expertise did not answer. The court did not accept every industry prediction as true; the unsupported agency response was the defect. Judge Robinson’s concurrence emphasized economic feasibility as part of statutory practicability. The notes explain that evidentiary and procedural failures overlap: the agency could reconsider and adopt an adequately supported rule. Congress’s express requirements survived even where the court’s practical doubts also applied to them, because APA rationality review concerns agency action and does not authorize rewriting the statute.
